title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations are references in AI papers that point to nonexistent works, or to real works with wrong authors, titles, or venues. Fact checking in this context means verifying that each citation resolves to a real publication and that extracted claims are supported by the cited source. The problem spans preprint servers, peer reviewed journals, and model generated text, and it undermines the reliability of literature reviews and meta analyses. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Fabricated citations are references in AI papers that point to nonexistent works, or to real works with wrong authors, titles, or venues. Fact checking in this context means verifying that each citation resolves to a real publication and that extracted claims are supported by the cited source. The problem spans preprint servers, peer reviewed journals, and model generated text, and it undermines the reliability of literature reviews and meta analyses. Within this site's library of 135 research papers and 10,767 extracted claims, citation integrity is treated as a core part of research quality rather than a clerical afterthought.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Fact checking runs on bibliographic databases, persistent identifiers such as DOIs, full text repositories, and reference parsers that break citations into structured fields. The site's practice of linking directly to the original paper, never to the Consensus search tool, means the infrastructure must resolve each reference to a stable source rather than a search result. Language models can assist in matching citation strings to records, but the underlying data layer is the authoritative check. Access to original papers, including paywalled or archived versions, is a practical constraint.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by extracting reference strings and claims from a paper, then normalizing author names, titles, years, and venues. Each citation is checked against a bibliographic record to confirm that the work exists and that the metadata matches. For claims, the relevant passage in the cited paper is located and compared with the claim as stated. Discrepancies are flagged for human review, since automated matching can miss subtle misattributions or context dependent meaning. The site's 10,767 extracted claims provide a structured set for testing these verification steps.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Risks include the spread of false findings, wasted effort by researchers who chase nonexistent sources, and damage to the credibility of authors and venues. Provenance requires that every claim trace back to the original paper, which is why this site links to the original paper and never to the Consensus search tool. Journals and preprint servers increasingly ask authors to provide DOIs or persistent identifiers, and some run automated checks before acceptance. Responsibility sits with authors, reviewers, and platform maintainers, but no single actor can catch every fabricated citation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Automated citation checking is likely to become a standard step in manuscript submission and preprint screening, with tools flagging suspicious references before peer review. Shared registries of retracted or fabricated citations could help researchers avoid citing known bad sources. As language models generate more reference lists, provenance standards will need to distinguish human verified citations from model suggested ones. Human review will remain necessary for claims that require interpretation, even as the volume of checks grows.
